problem.statement: Filtering large WPF DataGrids via ListCollectionView/CollectionView.Filter causes severe slowdowns and an unexplained large memory leak, and developers have no clear diagnosis or fix.

persona.primary: WPF developer building data-heavy line-of-business desktop apps

context.situation: A developer binds a DataGrid to ~37,000 items through a ListCollectionView and needs fast multi-column text filtering, but applying CollectionView.Filter in place is slow and leaks memory with no obvious cause.

current_workarounds: Discard the CollectionView.Filter approach and instead build a brand-new filtered ObservableCollection via LINQ on every filter change

possible_wedges.offer: A legacy WPF audit tool that scans/profiles a codebase for CollectionView.Filter memory-leak and performance antipatterns and reports flagged locations with fix guidance.
A drop-in NuGet library replacement for ListCollectionView that provides leak-free, fast multi-column filtering for large DataGrid-bound collections.
A paid one-off WPF performance audit: developer submits their CollectionView/DataGrid code and gets a diagnosed leak report plus a fix.

risks: Only a single evidence item from one developer; no indication of how widespread this is across legacy WPF audit clients
No commercial intent or willingness-to-pay signal present in the evidence
Root cause of the leak is unconfirmed (could be app-level misuse of CollectionView rather than a systemic framework issue worth productizing)
Evidence comes from a general WPF forum question, not from OwnAudit's actual audit-tooling customer base, so relevance to the audit-tool persona is an inference

cheapest_experiment.hypothesis: WPF developers maintaining large-dataset DataGrids hit CollectionView filter memory leaks often enough to want a free diagnostic or paid audit fix.
cheapest_experiment.input: Reply on the original thread (and similar WPF/DataGrid forum posts) with a technical explanation plus an offer of a free 'CollectionView leak checklist' in exchange for an email, linking to a paid audit option.
cheapest_experiment.output: Count of checklist requests (emails) and any replies asking about a paid audit or fix.
cheapest_experiment.commitment_event: Developer submits their email for the checklist or replies asking for the paid audit.
cheapest_experiment.success_threshold: At least 10% of thread viewers/repliers request the checklist or ask about the paid audit within 2 weeks.
cheapest_experiment.failure_threshold: Under 2% engagement or zero replies indicating willingness to pay within 2 weeks.
